books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: A Republican campaign broadside map of the United States, published in 1856, colors free states and slave states differently and draws a line across the western territories labeled as the Missouri Compromise line. The territories beyond the line are marked as lands “whose destiny is yet to be decided.”
stimulus.source_note: Map of the United States, showing by colors the area of freedom and slavery, published by G. W. Elliott, New York, 1856 (Republican campaign broadside; scan of pre-1930 original). Public domain.

source: original; stimulus is an 1856 Republican campaign broadside map showing the Missouri Compromise line (public domain, in the shared image pool as 5s24-ch14-mcq-01)
stem: The strongest reason to use this map carefully as evidence about the Missouri Compromise itself is that

options.text: maps from the 1850s never show state boundaries correctly enough to trust them
options.misconception: State boundaries are not the problem here; the map draws them well enough for its argument.

options.text: the map shows the compromise line in the wrong place
options.misconception: The line sits where the law put it, at 36°30′; the map’s geography is not the issue.

options.text: it was made by 1850s Republicans to argue a later case, thirty years on
the mapmaker had never visited the western territories
options.misconception: A mapmaker need not visit a place to draw a line fixed by law; travel is not the test here.

rationales.A: A map can be useful even with small boundary slips. The problem with this map is not its borders but its date and its purpose.
rationales.B: The line is drawn at 36°30′, where the Compromise put it. Check the argument, not the latitude, for the weakness.
rationales.C: The map is a Republican campaign broadside from 1856, made to argue about slavery's spread in its own decade. It shows how later Americans used the Compromise, not what the Compromise meant in 1820.
rationales.D: Mapmakers draw from surveys and laws, not from personal travel. Never having visited the West does not weaken a map of a legal line.
rationales.general:
1. Ask when the map was made. The 1850s, about thirty years after the Compromise.
2. Ask who made it and why. Republicans, to argue against slavery’s spread in their own decade.
3. Ask what that means for evidence. A later argument about the Compromise is not a record of the Compromise itself.
4. Put it together. The map is good evidence of 1850s Republican argument and weak evidence of 1820 intent.
Remember: date and purpose come before content when you judge a source.

figures.caption: Republican campaign broadside map of 1856 showing free and slave areas and the Missouri Compromise line
figures.alt: Map of the United States with free states and slave states in different colors, a line drawn across the western territories, and western lands labeled as not yet decided
